findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to the PR
findings.body: The change from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1` alters how often every background cleanup job runs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations), not just annotation cleanup. The PR description does not mention it, and it looks like a leftover debugging change. It raises the periodic DB load of all cleanup jobs roughly tenfold, and the annotation job can run for up to the 9-minute clean timeout. Revert it unless the new interval is an intentional, separately reviewed change.

findings.title: Routine batch progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: The informational logs added in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags use r.log.Error for every batch, including successful ones (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579). Every cleanup batch therefore emits error-level entries even when nothing failed. The 'Annotations to clean by time/count' and 'Tags to clean' entries also include the whole `ids` slice, up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs per line. With a large backlog this floods the error log with thousands of IDs and hides real errors. The `err` field logged at these points is always nil, because errors already return earlier. These should be Debug-level messages without the ID list.

findings.title: Quadratic string concatenation when building the inline SQLite ID list
findings.body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For a batch of up to 32767 IDs, which is the case the new test exercises, this copies on the order of several GB of bytes and performs tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup iteration. Build the list once with strings.Builder, strconv.AppendInt, or strings.Join over strconv.FormatInt.

findings.title: Non-SQLite delete now binds one parameter per ID, which breaks for large batch sizes
findings.body: The non-SQLite branch builds one `?` placeholder and one bind argument per ID. The previous DELETE only inlined LIMIT, so the statement did not depend on the batch size. MySQL prepared statements and the Postgres wire protocol reject more than 65535 bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is an unbounded int64 config value, so a batch size above that limit would make every cleanup batch fail on MySQL/Postgres, where it previously worked. Validate or cap the batch size, or chunk the DELETE IN list to a bounded number of parameters.
